newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Supreme Court keeps Tapie in jail.
newsitem.headline: French Supreme Court keeps Tapie in jail.

text.p: France's Supreme Court rejected a last-ditch appeal by bankrupt former politician and soccer boss Bernard Tapie on Tuesday against an eight-month jail sentence for rigging a soccer match.

The ruling means that the fallen tycoon and former left-wing cabinet minister, convicted of bribery and interfering with witnesses, must stay in prison. He turned himself in at Paris' La Sante jail on Monday night.

Tapie's lawyer, Jean-Yves Lienard, told reporters his client would immediately resign from the European Parliament before the Strasbourg-based assembly can strip him of his Radical party seat at the French government's request on February 17.
He has already been stripped of his seat in the French National Assembly.

Tapie was not in court to hear his lawyer urge the Cour de Cassation to quash his conviction for rigging a 1993 first division match between his Marseille club and rival Valenciennes a few days before his team won the 1993 European Cup.

The lawyer challenged the legal classification of the offences as "corruption" and "interfering with witnesses" and argued that the lower court had no right to send him to jail as he was still at that time a member of the National Assembly.

Lawyers say Tapie, who has confessed to being terrified of going to jail, may be entitled to serve most of his term in an open prison, spending the nights in his freshly-repainted cell and being allowed out by day to work in his new profession as a film actor.

He may also be eligible for parole for good behaviour after serving half his term. But he will be in the box again twice in March to answer charges of tax fraud and of corruption in connection with the finances of Marseille.
The 54-year-old rags-to-riches businessman evaded photographers when he turned himself in to prison authorities on Monday evening.

Hidden under a blanket in the back of his son's car, he was driven to the Quai des Orfevres police headquarters, where he was put into a white prison bus with frosted windows and taken to La Sante prison in central Paris.
Prisoner number 265 449 G, incarcerated on his own in the prison's VIP wing, was the top story in all French newspapers.

Ironically, his cell is near that of businessman Pierre Botton, convicted of sleaze and misuse of corporate funds, who accuses Tapie of engineering his downfall. Lienard said the two men were bound to meet in the prison yard.
